module_title: Advanced Articles - Vetoes, Deadlocks, and Judicial Nuances
introduction: This advanced level explores the subtle constitutional friction points between the Union and States. It covers the executive's assent to bills, the creation of legislative councils, and the extraordinary powers of the Supreme Court.

core_concepts.title: Assent to Bills (Art 111 vs. Art 200)
core_concepts.description: Article 111 deals with the President's assent to Parliament's bills (veto power). Article 200 deals with the Governor's assent to state bills. Crucially, under Art 200, the Governor can 'reserve the bill for the consideration of the President'.

core_concepts.title: President's Assent on State Bills (Article 201)
core_concepts.description: Once a Governor reserves a bill under Art 200, Article 201 kicks in. The President can give assent, withhold it, or return it. Unlike central bills, the President is NOT bound to give assent even if the state legislature passes it a second time.

core_concepts.title: Creation/Abolition of Legislative Councils (Article 169)
core_concepts.description: Provides the mechanism to create or abolish the Upper House (Vidhan Parishad) in a state. It requires a special majority in the State Assembly and a simple majority in the Parliament.

core_concepts.title: Supreme Court's 'Complete Justice' (Article 142)
core_concepts.description: An extraordinary power that allows the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any matter pending before it. This is the legal basis for much of the court's judicial activism.

core_concepts.title: Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143)
core_concepts.description: Allows the President to consult the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact of public importance. The SC's opinion is not binding on the President.

important_entities.name: Constitutional Discretion (Article 163)
important_entities.significance: Under Article 74, the President is bound by the aid and advice of the CoM. However, Article 163 explicitly grants the Governor 'discretionary powers' where they are not bound by the state CoM.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Remember the sequence: The Governor reserves the bill under Article 200. The President acts upon that reserved bill under Article 201. Exams often swap these.

While Art 32 (Supreme Court) is a fundamental right itself, Art 226 (High Court) is not. However, Art 226 grants a wider scope to High Courts because they can issue writs for legal rights, not just fundamental rights.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Article 200 parks/reserves the bill for the center. Article 201 is where the President actually decides on it.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Assertion-Reasoning questions, deeply understand the difference in language between Art 74 (Union) and Art 163 (State) regarding discretionary powers.
Article 142 is highly relevant in current affairs (used for Babri Masjid verdict, banning liquor near highways, etc.). Expect questions on its scope.
